Cox proportional hazards models revealed predation (accounting for 68% of mortality events, primarily by mustelids and raptors) and late-season precipitation extremes as dominant mortality drivers. Juveniles in pastures with >40% native grass cover exhibited 1.7× higher survival (HR = 0.59, 95% CI: 0.43–0.81) compared to those in reseeded hayfields, mediated through reduced predator detection probabilities in structurally complex vegetation. An anomalous 2019 drought year reduced survival by 22% relative to baseline levels, with carryover effects decreasing first-year breeding site fidelity (r = 0.71, p < 0.01). Our results demonstrate that conversion of heterogeneous native grasslands to homogeneous agricultural landscapes imposes fitness costs on this declining grassland obligate. Targeted retention of >30 cm vegetation height within 200 m of nest sites could enhance juvenile recruitment by 18–24%, providing a scalable management strategy to mitigate habitat fragmentation impacts. These findings underscore the importance of incorporating post-fledging dynamics into population viability models for temperate grassland songbirds.
